evidence_locator: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22770963/
notes: [Verified 2026-03-17 | J Am Coll Surg 2012 | content_match] Philip Syng Physick (1768-1837), called the 'Father of American Surgery,' was elected the first professor of surgery at the University of Pennsylvania in 1805 — the first such chair in the United States. He held it until 1819 when he transferred to the anatomy chair (retiring 1831). Trained in London under John Hunter at St. George's Hospital (1788-1790), he was Hunter's first American house surgeon. He pioneered catgut sutures, the stomach pump, and tonsillectomy instruments. He was surgeon to Pennsylvania Hospital from 1794 to 1816 and treated Chief Justice John Marshall and First Lady Dolley Madison. His lectures prepared an entire generation of American surgeons. This edge extends the UPenn surgery lineage 140 years before Ravdin (1945), establishing an independent pre-Halsted Philadelphia surgical trunk. Physick and Halsted represent two distinct origin points for American academic surgery: Philadelphia (1805) and Baltimore (1889). [V17-B2 C1 correction: end_year 1831 -> 1819 so the edge encodes the surgery-chair tenure only, per the chair-tenure convention; the notes above already stated the 1819 transfer and the 1819-1831 anatomy professorship remains documented here. Whether PMID 22770963 full text states the 1819 transfer is unconfirmed (content-match ceiling); if the implementer's full-text read confirms it the PMID evidence tier stands as-is, otherwise it still stands for the founding/Hunter facts with the chair-transfer date resting on Penn Archives (archives.upenn.edu/exhibits/penn-people/biography/philip-syng-physick).]

notes: [Verified 2026-03-17 | Ann Surg 1980 | content_match] Gross served as professor of surgery at Jefferson from 1856 to 1882, succeeding Thomas Dent Mutter. He was called the 'Emperor of American Surgery' and published 14 books and over 1,200 articles. During this tenure he founded the Philadelphia Academy of Surgery (1879, the oldest continuously meeting surgical society in the US) and the American Surgical Association (1880, already in graph via graph_update_draft.json). He also served as AMA president (1868). His successor was William W. Keen, who became one of the first surgeons to operate on the brain (1889). The dual edges (Jefferson trained Gross; Gross led Jefferson) create a bidirectional circuit rare in the graph and mirror the pattern seen in Cincinnati (where Altemeier returned to lead the department that trained him).

evidence_locator: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22770963/
notes: [Verified 2026-03-17 | J Am Coll Surg 2012 | content_match] Philip Syng Physick (1768-1837) traveled to London in 1788 to study under John Hunter at St. George's Hospital, where he learned anatomy from cadaver dissection. On January 1, 1790, Hunter appointed Physick house surgeon — the first American to hold that position at St. George's. Physick received the diploma of the Royal College of Surgeons in 1790 and dedicated his Edinburgh MD thesis on apoplexy to Hunter (1792). Hunter offered Physick a partnership, but Physick returned to Philadelphia in 1792 and was appointed first professor of surgery at the University of Pennsylvania in 1805. Sheldon (JACS 2012) titles Physick explicitly as Hunter's favorite American trainee. This bridge edge merges the Hunter/Cline island (Component 9, 2 nodes in 14_global_military) into the main component via Physick's existing edges in 13_pre_halsted, extending the graph's temporal depth from 1777 (Hunter-Cline) through the entire pre-Halsted American trunk (Physick 1805, Gross 1828, ASA 1880) to the Halstedian era.
